pathwayLabel: Certification by Endorsement — 10-Year Licensure History (Option C) — Reciprocity Not Available for This Classification
steps: Florida's Reciprocity form (DBPR CILB 32, limited to Louisiana, Mississippi, and North Carolina) offers no Air-Conditioning category at all, so reciprocity is unavailable to HVAC contractors in Florida regardless of home state. Ohio and Florida also have no reciprocity agreement with each other.
The applicable route is DBPR CILB 10, Certification by Endorsement (Section 489.115(3), Florida Statutes), which lists Class A and Class B Air-Conditioning as selectable categories.

Within CILB 10, the NASCLA-based route does not apply — the form restricts it to General, Building, and Residential licenses. The practical route for an Ohio HVAC contractor is Option C: hold a valid, current out-of-state contracting license for at least 10 years, active now or within the last 2 years, of a license type 'the same or similar as the license type being applied for.'

needs_review: Ohio's HVAC contractor license and Florida's Class A/B Air-Conditioning certification are both state contractor licenses, so Ohio's is plausibly 'similar' — but Ohio's license covers commercial work only, while Florida's Class A is unrestricted. Whether that satisfies Option C, and whether it maps to Class A or Class B, is CILB's determination.

needs_review: CILB 10's 2-hour Florida Building Code course requirement is scoped to General, Building, Residential, and Roofing applicants only — Air-Conditioning is not listed. Whether AC applicants face this requirement is not stated in the document and is not assumed here.

Submit verification of licensure showing at least 10 years and any discipline, a copy of Ohio's statutes/rules defining the HVAC contractor license, electronic fingerprints, a FICO-derived credit report, and proof of satisfaction of any liens, judgments, or bankruptcy.
Pay the $350 Endorsement application fee to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
Await processing — DBPR does not publish a guaranteed timeline; budget for several weeks to a few months.
notes: Florida-side forms confirmed 2026-09-30 by antiword extraction of the versions incorporated in Rule 61-35.010, F.A.C. (effective 2026-06-28), downloaded from flrules.org: CILB 32 (Reciprocity, Ref-17723) lists Louisiana, Mississippi, and North Carolina for General/Building/Residential only, with no Air-Conditioning category; CILB 10 (Endorsement, Ref-17718) lists Class A and Class B Air-Conditioning, $350 fee, Options A/B/C for all categories, NASCLA limited to General/Building/Residential, 2-hour Building Code course scoped to General/Building/Residential/Roofing. Option C requires 'at least 10 years' of out-of-state licensure, active within the last 2 years, and that 'the license type must be the same or similar as the license type being applied for.' Ohio side: OCILB's Out-of-State Examination Application (form dated 9/2025, dam.assets.ohio.gov) states OCILB 'issues state licenses to Electrical, HVAC, Refrigeration, Plumbing, and Hydronics Contractors who perform commercial work', and the license must be assigned to a contracting company — i.e. a contractor-level license, the same level as Florida's certification. No Florida agreement exists among OCILB's published per-state reciprocity agreements (404 for a Florida file; HVAC agreements are with AL, KY, LA, MS, SC, TN, WV). needs_review: the 'same or similar' judgment (Ohio commercial-only vs. Florida's unrestricted Class A) is CILB's and is not resolved by either form; the 2-hour course question carries over from the other Florida HVAC records.
officialSourceName: Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation, Construction Industry Licensing Board (DBPR CILB)
